question: How do Japanese housemakers build prefabricated houses that are both high quality and economical?

answer.answer:
Quality in prefabricated housing is reached by two cited routes, industrialised production (AT8) and prefabrication/off-site work (PR2), both resting on the same upstream requirement of highly standardised components (AT7), which in turn opens the way to a kit-of-parts configurator (AR6), modular architecture (AT2) and robotic assembly (PR4). Economy is much thinner in the record: reduce cost (VA6) is drawn on by 22 of the 50 coded cases, but the single cited dependency reaching it is robotic assembly amplifying it, carried by only 7 of the 50, so the cost side of the pairing is asserted far less firmly than the quality side. In practice that means standardise first, industrialise the line, and expect the cost case to rest on your own production economics rather than on published dependency; watch design compromise from over-standardisation (RI15), production/assembly restriction (RI19) and the reliance on precise planning (RI14), which 36 of the 50 cases carry. The eleven deployed records at the housemaker stakeholder tier support this, though the record does not use the terms "Japanese housemakers" or "houses" as such and names no firm behind them.

**The quality route is the better-evidenced one.** VA3 "Improve quality/performance" carries 2 inbound and 0 outbound dependency edges, and 37 of the 50 coded cases draw on it [1], so the two routes below are the complete cited set. The first is industrialisation: industrialised production (AT8) enables improve quality/performance (VA3), on the finding that quality-oriented industrialised production considerably increases housing quality by providing standard fittings [2], backed by peer-reviewed evidence and carried by 22 of the 50 coded cases [1]. The second is the factory itself: prefabrication/off-site (PR2) enables improve quality/performance (VA3) through the controlled factory environment [3], carried by 18 of the 50 [1]. Prefabrication also carries quality indirectly, since it enables reduce errors/constraints (VA10) by improving quality control and reducing rework [4] (14 of the 50 [1]), and enables improve site safety (VA13) by moving work offsite [5] (12 of the 50 [1]).

**Standardisation is the requirement under both.** In `AT8 dependsOn AT7`, standardisation is upstream: industrialised-construction scale depends on highly standardised components, carried by 16 of the 50 [1], and 25 of the 50 cases draw on AT7 "Highly standardised" [1]. From there AT7 runs outward to six things, of which the strongest carried are reduce construction complexity (VA7), carried by 15 [1], DfMA for DFAB process (PR9), carried by 13 [1], configurators/kit-of-parts (AR6), carried by 11 [1] and modular architecture (AT2), carried by 11 [1]. The one that matters for automation is AT7 enabling robotic assembly (PR4), on the finding that Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components [6], carried by 10 of the 50 [1]. The counterweight is that AT7 also enables accommodate late design changes (VA21), and that edge is carried by only 2 of the 50 [1], which is where the over-standardisation risk bites: 17 of the 50 draw on RI15 "Design compromise/over standardised", and it carries no dependency edge at all [1], so the literature has not connected it even though the record shows it plainly.

**The cost side.** VA6 "Reduce cost" carries 1 inbound and 0 outbound edges and is drawn on by 22 of the 50 [1]; that single edge is robotic assembly (PR4) amplifying reduce cost, carried by 7 of the 50 [1], with the same process also amplifying reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency (VA2), carried by 13 [1]. Robotic assembly itself is drawn on by 13 of the 50 [1] and has two well-carried requirements of its own: it depends on a robotic arm (RE2), carried by 12 [1], and it has prefabrication/off-site (PR2) as a precondition, because automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [7], carried by 4 of the 50 [1]. Of PR4's cited requirements, then, the machine is common in the record and the prefabrication precondition is rarely carried alongside it. Cost uncertainty is separately visible: 13 of the 50 draw on RI3 "Increase cost/investment uncertainty" [1], and the one cited mitigation is traceable/linked data (VA9) mitigating it, carried by 7 of the 50 [1].

**What the deployed records show.** Eleven deployed cases carry the housemaker stakeholder tier: RP17, RP2, RP29, RP32, RP45, RP49, RP5, RP50, RP6, RP8 and RP9, which is the complete set for that value [8]. Three of them were adopted against cost and quality together. RP2 works on the structural core with assembly, heavy lift, steel welding and steelwork in steel, adopted to address Cost and Quality, at technology readiness level 9 [8]. RP32 does surface welding, steelwork and surface treatment in steel, adopted to address Cost, Labor, Quality and Safety, at technology readiness level 9 [8], and RP50 does steelwork in steel against Cost, Digital, Labor and Quality, also at technology readiness level 9 [8]. The pattern across the tier is a standardised structural product line in a single material family, mostly steel and timber, at full deployment maturity: RP49 combines material handling with timber joinery cutting against Digital, Labor and Quality [8], and RP29 does facade assembly and tiling against Labor, Market, Quality and Safety [8]. Two caveats on reading these: the context gives no firm for any of them, and it does not link any of these records to the enablers above, so the AT7 to AT8 to VA3 chain is evidence from the coded case counts and the literature, not from these eleven records individually.

**What to watch beyond the edges.** 36 of the 50 cases draw on RI14 "Rely on precise planning" [1], the requirement under prefabrication: PR2 depends on it, carried by 18 of the 50 [1]. 25 of the 50 draw on RI19 "Production/assembly restriction", which carries no cited edge [1], and 14 draw on RI1 "Increase uncertainty in production", likewise unconnected [1]. Regulation is a live dependency rather than a background condition: PR2 depends on regulatory/legal concern (RI18), carried by 10 of the 50, where offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability [1]. And the organisational precondition should not be skipped: industrialisation depends on delivery/business model/work culture (RI12), carried by 13 of the 50 [1], while vertical integration (CO10) enables industrialisation, carried by 17 [1] and early contractor involvement (CO11) enables prefabrication, carried by 13 [1]. Finally, the strongest single fact in the record sits outside the edge layer entirely: RE6 "Significant human involvement" is drawn on by all 50 coded cases and has no cited edge [1], so the economics of these lines are not those of unattended automation.
